pr.title: Remove semi-nondeterminism of `DefPathHash` ordering from inliner
pr.description:
Déjà vu or something because I kinda thought I had put this PR up before. I recall a discussion somewhere where I think it was @saethlin mentioning that this check was no longer needed since we have "proper" cycle detection. Putting that up as a PR now.

This may slighlty negatively affect inlining, since the cycle breaking here means that we still inlined some cycles when the def path hashes were ordered in certain ways, this leads to really bad nondeterminism that makes minimizing ICEs and putting up inliner bugfixes difficult.

r? @cjgillot or @saethlin or someone else idk
pr.author: compiler-errors

analysis.summary: Fixes semi-nondeterministic inlining of recursive/mutually-recursive local calls by deleting the inliner's `DefPathHash`-ordering early return and relying on the existing `mir_callgraph_reachable` cycle check. The old hash-based cycle breaker inlined some cycles only when caller/callee hashes happened to be ordered a certain way, making MIR output and ICE minimization unstable. This changed test expectations: `f::<fn() {g}>` is no longer inlined into `main` in the `cycle` test, and the generic cycle test no longer produces the deeper `scope 4`/`scope 5` inlined scopes.
analysis.originalLogic: In `compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/inline.rs`, for local callees, the inliner first used `DefPathHash` ordering to avoid cycles: if `self.tcx.def_path_hash(caller_def_id).local_hash() < self.tcx.def_path_hash(callee_def_id).local_hash()`, it returned `Ok(())` and skipped inlining. The comment claimed this would ensure the callee would not inline the caller and that the trick works with incremental compilation because `DefPathHash` is stable. Only after that check did it test `self.tcx.mir_callgraph_reachable((callee, caller_def_id.expect_local()))` to avoid inlining a function known to call back.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical behavior made the inlining decision for cyclic local calls depend on the relative ordering of stable `DefPathHash` values rather than only on real call-graph reachability. When the caller hash was not less than the callee hash, the hash-based early return did not fire, so the inliner could still inline a recursive or mutually-recursive call. The PR explicitly states that "we still inlined some cycles when the def path hashes were ordered in certain ways", producing semi-nondeterminism. The fix removes the hash comparison block entirely so cycle avoidance is handled solely by `mir_callgraph_reachable`, changing both deterministic inlining behavior and MIR test output.
analysis.inputDomain: The MIR `Inline` pass on local (`callee_def_id.is_local()`) calls whose call graph contains a recursive or mutually-recursive cycle, including generic instantiations. Observable via `tests/mir-opt/inline/*` `Inline` MIR dumps under both `panic-abort` and `panic-unwind`. Relevant to incremental compilation because `DefPathHash` is stable across builds, which is exactly why the old heuristic appeared deterministic but was not semantically meaningful.
analysis.trigger: A local call in a recursive or mutually recursive call graph where the old `DefPathHash` comparison would allow inlining, for example `f(g)` where `f` is generic over a function item that can call back, or generic `Call` impls forming an A/B/C cycle. With the old code, hash ordering can cause additional `scope N (inlined ...)` scopes that disappear after removal.
preconditions: The caller/callee call graph contains a cycle or mutual recursion, including through generic instantiations.
The caller and callee have stable `DefPathHash` values, as in incremental compilation.
The `Inline` MIR pass is run and its output is inspected with MIR dumps for both panic strategies.
pitfalls: Do not treat `DefPathHash` ordering as a semantic property of the call graph; using it to break cycles makes inlining depend on irrelevant stable hashes.
Removing the hash check changes which cycles are inlined, so it is not merely a performance-neutral cleanup; test expectations legitimately change.
Do not remove or weaken the `mir_callgraph_reachable` check when deleting the hash-ordering block; that reachability check is the proper cycle detection.
A retained test file name or old CHECK comment does not prove inlining still occurs; compare actual MIR assignments and `scope (inlined ...)` entries.
The mir-opt `.diff` files have two layers: the outer patch edits test expectations, while inner `+`/`-` lines describe MIR before/after the Inline pass.
`panic-abort` and `panic-unwind` outputs differ in unwind/cleanup blocks, so both expectations must be updated consistently.
Distinguish lack of inlining due to cycle avoidance from other bailouts such as cost or attributes.
analysis.testStrategy: Use/extend `tests/mir-opt/inline/cycle.rs` and `tests/mir-opt/inline/inline_cycle_generic.rs`, emitting the `Inline` MIR dump and running both panic-abort and panic-unwind. Assert that cyclic calls such as `f(g)` remain calls (`_1 = f::<fn() {g}>(g)`) and that no extra `scope N (inlined ...)` for the cyclic generic recursion is produced. Construct two equivalent programs differing only in whether the old `DefPathHash` ordering gate is present, and verify the resulting MIR is invariant to hash ordering. Also retain a control case where a non-cyclic local call still inlines, so the test distinguishes cycle avoidance from a general inlining regression.
